title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 30
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Years That Do Not Divide
passages.text:
A. Every calendar is an attempt to reconcile three cycles that do not fit together. The day, the lunar month and the solar year are set by independent physical processes, and none is a whole-number multiple of another. A calendar is therefore not a discovery about time but a negotiated compromise about which mismatch to tolerate, and every society has had to choose which one to push into the corners.

B. Calendars that follow the moon keep months honest and let the year drift. Because twelve lunar months fall short of a solar year by roughly eleven days, a purely lunar calendar moves steadily through the seasons, so that a given month occurs in summer and, some years later, in winter. For a community whose year is organised around observance rather than harvest this is tolerable; for one that must plant at the right time it is not.

C. Calendars that follow the sun keep the seasons fixed and abandon the moon. Months become administrative divisions with no astronomical meaning, and the price is arbitrariness: their unequal lengths are the residue of political decisions rather than of anything in the sky. Most agricultural societies made this trade, and the irregularity that results is the visible scar of the compromise.

D. The residual error is where the interesting engineering lies. A solar year is close to but not exactly three hundred and sixty-five and a quarter days, so a leap day every fourth year over-corrects slightly, and the accumulated excess moves the seasons by about three days every four centuries. Detecting an error that small required centuries of records, and correcting it required omitting leap years in certain century years — a rule that looks fussy and is the minimum necessary.

E. Implementing the correction was a political operation rather than an astronomical one. Days had to be deleted from the calendar to restore the alignment already lost, and states adopted the change across a span of centuries according to whose authority had proposed it, so that for a long period neighbouring countries disagreed about the date. Contracts, ages and anniversaries had to be translated between systems, and historical dates from the period still require care.

F. What the whole history illustrates is the cost of a standard adopted unevenly. The arithmetic was settled long before the adoption was, and the delay produced expense and confusion out of all proportion to the technical problem. A shared measure is worth more than an accurate one that only some people use, which is a lesson that applies well beyond the counting of days.

passages.title: Living Without Drinking
passages.text:
The problem a desert sets is not heat but water, and the two are connected in a way that constrains every solution. The standard mammalian response to heat is evaporation — sweating or panting — which works well and spends the resource that is scarcest. An animal that cools itself this way in a place with no water to replace the loss has solved one problem by worsening another, which is why the most successful desert animals mostly do not cool themselves this way.

Avoidance does more work than physiology. The great majority of desert mammals are active at night and spend the day in burrows, where the temperature is moderate and the humidity is far higher than at the surface. A burrow a metre down converts a lethal environment into a survivable one at no metabolic cost, and much of what looks like remarkable physiological tolerance is in fact remarkable behavioural avoidance of the conditions that would require it.

Some species have dispensed with drinking altogether, which is the most striking adaptation and the most misunderstood. Water is produced by metabolism itself — burning food yields water as a product — and an animal that loses very little can live on that alone. The achievement is therefore not in generating water but in not losing it: highly concentrated urine, dry faeces, no sweating, and a nasal arrangement that recovers moisture from exhaled air before it leaves the body.

The large animals that cannot hide have taken a different route. An animal too big for a burrow can instead allow its body temperature to rise substantially during the day and fall again at night, storing heat rather than spending water to dissipate it. This is only available to animals with enough mass to heat slowly, and it requires tolerating internal temperatures that would be dangerous in a species that had not evolved to expect them.

Plants face the same accounting with fewer options, since they cannot move or shelter. Their solutions are correspondingly extreme: opening pores only at night, storing water in tissue, shedding leaves in drought, or completing an entire life cycle in the weeks following rain and passing the remaining years as seed. The last is the most complete answer to the problem — it does not survive the desert so much as decline to be present for it.

The general lesson is that adaptation to an extreme environment is usually less exotic than it appears. The mechanisms are ordinary ones pushed to their limits, combined with behaviour that avoids the extreme rather than confronting it, and the animals that appear to defy the conditions are mostly the ones that have arranged not to experience them.

passages.title: What the Seller Knows
passages.text:
Some markets fail for a reason that has nothing to do with monopoly, regulation or irrationality. When a seller knows more about the quality of an item than a buyer can determine before purchase, and the buyer knows this, the buyer will not pay the price a good item deserves — because from the buyer's position a good item and a bad one look identical. The offered price settles towards what an average item is worth.

The consequence unravels the market rather than merely lowering its prices. Owners of genuinely good items, unable to obtain a price reflecting quality, withdraw and keep them; the average quality of what remains for sale therefore falls; buyers, observing this, lower what they will pay further; and more of the better items withdraw. The logic can continue until only the worst items are traded, or until no market exists at all, and it requires no dishonesty from anyone.

Second-hand vehicles are the standard illustration and the effect appears wherever the same conditions hold. Insurance markets face it in reverse, since the buyer knows more about their own risk than the insurer; credit markets face it in the borrower's knowledge of their own intentions; and labour markets face a version of it in the difficulty of assessing a worker before employment. The structure, not the commodity, produces the problem.

What prevents the collapse in practice is a set of institutions that exist precisely to make quality visible. Warranties transfer the risk back to the seller and are credible because a seller who knows the item is bad would not offer one. Reputation works where transactions repeat and where the seller has an identity that persists. Independent inspection and certification substitute a third party's assessment for the buyer's ignorance. Each is expensive, and the expense is the cost of the underlying information problem.

Understanding this changes what regulation is for. Requirements to disclose service history, restrictions on selling without a warranty, and licensing of intermediaries look like interference in a transaction between consenting parties, and are more usefully read as attempts to make a market possible that would otherwise operate badly or not at all. The alternative to the regulated market is frequently not a freer market but a smaller one.

The same analysis explains why some things are not sold at all. Where quality cannot be verified, cannot be guaranteed, and the transaction does not repeat, no institution bridges the gap, and the exchange simply does not happen even though both parties would gain from it. The absence of a market is sometimes evidence of an information problem rather than of an absence of demand.
